ARCTANGENT → POLE NORMALIZATION → RESIDUES

Arctangent, residues and Cauchy’s formula

A square contour turns the Cauchy kernel into the same rational function that computes our geometric π.

PNT+ formalizes this rectangle route to the residue theorem. Here we follow its mathematics, connect the pole normalization to our rational interval foundation, and separate the checked results from the remaining native bridges.

Scope. The square-pole computation below is checked natively, without Mathlib. PNT+ supplies the external formal reference for general rectangles and finitely many simple poles. A full native residue theorem and Cauchy integral formula are still to be constructed.

One side of a square is an arctangent

Take the counterclockwise boundary of the square [−1,1]². On its right side, put z = 1 + iu. Rational complex division gives

dz/z = (u + i)/(1 + u²) du.

The real contribution is odd in u. Pair the lower and upper halves, then rotate through the other three sides. All eight oriented half-edges reduce to one real integral:

∮∂□ dz/z = 8i ∫₀¹ du/(1 + u²) = 8i A(1) = 2πi.

On a translated square z = p + rw, the factors r cancel in dz/(z−p). Any nonzero rational real scale r therefore gives the same normalization, including a negative r, which rotates the square by a half turn.

The finite computation behind the integral

Checked here · rational interval foundation

Each stage subdivides [0,1] into 2ⁿ cells. The kernel 1/(1+u²) decreases, so endpoint rectangles enclose every choice of tags on that partition. The imaginary interval has an explicit width bound:

widthRe(Iₙ) = 0,   widthIm(Iₙ) ≤ 16/2ⁿ.

The boxes are nested and valid. Their equivalence to 2πi follows from the existing geometric arctangent comparison. π remains piCircleArea; the contour computation is an alternative representation of its multiple.

The regular part contributes zero

Suppose a rectangle contains p in its interior and

f(z) = g(z) + a/(z − p).

If g is holomorphic throughout the rectangle, its boundary integral vanishes. The pole contributes 2πia, giving

∮∂Ω f(z) dz = 2πi a.

In PNT+, the side primitives contain both logarithms and arctangents. The logarithmic terms cancel, and reciprocal-arctangent identities give the constant 2πi. Rectangle subdivision also transports a pole computation to a smaller rectangle around the pole. Summing finitely many principal parts yields the finite simple-pole residue theorem.

PNT+ assumes meromorphicity, finitely many poles, no boundary poles and simple poles for its checked finite-sum theorem. Commented-out generalizations are not checked results.

Cauchy’s value formula is a residue calculation

Apply the simple-pole argument to F(z)/(z−p). Its decomposition is

F(z)/(z−p) = [F(z)−F(p)]/(z−p) + F(p)/(z−p).

The divided difference extends across p with value F′(p). A local series makes this explicit: subtract the constant coefficient and shift the remaining coefficients down by one. This supplies the regular part; the residue is F(p).

∮∂Ω F(z)/(z−p) dz = 2πi F(p).

This is the mathematical deduction we would reconstruct natively with certified charts and contour computations. It is not an additional native theorem asserted by this page.

PNT+ also explicitly proves cauchy_formula_deriv, with a squared denominator on a circle. That declaration invokes Mathlib’s circle-integral derivative theorem directly. Its formal dependency path is separate from the rectangle/arctangent route.

What the full native adaptation needs

The same mathematics fits explicit computation, but each passage from finite sums to a contour value needs its own bound.

  1. Vanishing of the regular part. Supply local chart or affine-remainder bounds. Cancel shared edges of a finite grid. A quadratic error M/N² on each unit-square cell gives contour error at most 4M/N.
  2. Transport past the poles. Exhibit a finite rectangle-with-holes subdivision and positive rational distances from its cells to the poles. Connect its cancellation identity to the actual outer and inner integral computations.
  3. Remove principal parts. Compute the regular remainder, certify the divided-difference extension and prove contour linearity. These are proof obligations, not assumed fields naming the desired result.

The checked square normalization supplies the constant and a nonzero bound. It does not yet discharge these general bridges.
